pages.text: Expansionism means a state gets more control over land. This often happens through direct taking of land, military empires, or colonies. In past times, the reason for taking land was very simple. Countries took land just because they could do it.

Over time, political ideas changed. Leaders started to use more complex reasons to take land. Sometimes, countries try to take back lost areas. They might claim these were their ancestral lands. Other times, they talk about promised lands.

Many parts of the world have seen expansionism. In history, the Ottoman Empire entered a time of growth. They ended the Eastern Roman Empire when they took Constantinople in the year 1453 under Mehmed the Conqueror.

Russia also had periods of expansion under leaders like Czar Nicholas I. His reign led to wars against Persia and Turkey. Troops also went into Austria-Hungary to stop a revolt. Later, Russia invaded Crimea.

Today, several nations are still described as expansionist by analysts. Russia has occupied parts of neighboring countries like Georgia and Ukraine. Meanwhile, China has claims in the South China Sea.

pages.text: Other countries are also involved in expansion. Turkey has stationed troops in foreign lands following various military actions. The United States has also seen proposals to expand its influence and territory in modern times.

Expansionism refers to states obtaining greater control of territories, often through direct annexation, military empire-building, or colonialism. During the classical age of conquest, the moral justification for expanding at the expense of another polity was often unapologetic, relying on the philosophy that might makes right.

As political ideas evolved around the rights of the governed, more complex justifications emerged. States sometimes use anarchy, reunification, or pan-nationalism to legitimize reconquering lost territories. Lacking historical claims, would-be expansionists may promote ideologies of promised lands and self-interested pragmatism.

History shows numerous examples across every region. The Ottoman Empire expanded significantly during the 15th and 16th centuries, culminating in the conquest of Constantinople in 1453 by Mehmed the Conqueror, which ended the Eastern Roman Empire.

During the 19th century, the reign of Russian Czar Nicholas I led to several wars of conquest against Persia and Turkey, along with the suppression of revolts in Europe and the Caucasus. Later, pan-Slavist solidarity provoked further conflict with the Ottoman Empire.

In modern times, several nations face accusations of expansionism. Russia under Vladimir Putin has occupied parts of Georgia and annexed territories from Ukraine since the 2010s. China has also faced similar descriptions regarding its operations and claims in the South China Sea.

pages.text: Turkey has pursued an aggressive foreign policy involving military presence and occupations in neighboring regions like Cyprus, Syria, and Iraq. Additionally, American political figures have occasionally proposed plans to expand national influence and acquire new territories.

Expansionism denotes the acquisition of greater territorial control by states, predominantly executed through direct annexation, imperial conquest, or colonialism. In classical antiquity, the philosophical justification for territorial aggrandizement at the expense of established polities frequently invoked unapologetic doctrines of realpolitik and might makes right.

Concurrently, the evolution of political conceptions regarding governance engendered sophisticated rationalizations for territorial expansion. Modern or historical justifications frequently incorporate state collapse, reunification, and pan-nationalism to reclaim perceived ancestral domains, while lacking such rationales, actors occasionally deploy teleological ideologies of promised lands.

Historical manifestations span globally. The Ottoman Empire exemplified this trajectory during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, most notably through Mehmed the Conqueror taking Constantinople in 1453, thereby terminating the Eastern Roman Empire.

Similarly, the militarist reign of Russian Czar Nicholas I catalyzed extensive wars against Persia and Turkey, alongside the military suppression of regional rebellions and subsequent conflicts driven by pan-Slavist solidarity.

Contemporary geopolitics continues to feature expansionist dynamics. Russian foreign policy under Vladimir Putin has incorporated the annexation and occupation of territories in Georgia and Ukraine, while the People's Republic of China faces concurrent designations regarding maritime assertions in the South China Sea.
